body: Deploying Product Forge SaaS or Enterprise editions currently requires executing multiple manual steps (database migration, object store setup, environment configuration, service runner startup). A turnkey enterprise product requires an automated one-command infrastructure-as-code deployment pipeline. This item provides the official Helm chart and Terraform modules.

brief.why: Manual platform deployment is error-prone, violates reproducible delivery standards, and impedes turnkey commercial customer rollouts.
brief.problem: Plane A (Product Forge platform itself) lacks an automated turnkey one-click cloud provisioning bundle (Helm chart + Terraform), requiring manual database and cluster configuration.
brief.what_adds: Plane A One-Click Cloud Provisioner: Helm chart and Terraform modules for automated Product Forge cluster deployment.
brief.who_feels: Platform DevOps engineers, enterprise cloud administrators, and deployment operators

label: PF Backlog 690
risks: Cloud provider API rate limits during infrastructure provisioning mitigated via idempotent Terraform state.

design_pack.title: Plane A One-Click Cloud Provisioner: Helm chart and Terraform modules for automated Product Forge cluster deployment
design_pack.quotas: Resource requests: 500m CPU, 1Gi memory per API pod; limits: 2 CPU, 4Gi memory

rollout.strategy: Canary / RollingUpdate deployment for API pods

coverage.contract: Helm chart deploys complete Product Forge platform stack including PostgreSQL with pgvector, object store, and core API pods with persistent volume retention
failure_cases: missing values or invalid image tag fails template generation
coverage.failure_behavior: fail fast on missing templates or invalid syntax

coverage.contract: Terraform module automates cloud VPC, managed Kubernetes cluster, and HA database provisioning across AWS and GCP providers
failure_cases: missing provider credentials or quota limits abort provisioning
coverage.failure_behavior: fail fast on quota limit or credentials missing

coverage.contract: Single command deployment script provisions infrastructure, deploys Helm chart, and passes automated post-deploy health check in under 10 minutes on warm clusters (25 minutes for cold cloud cluster provisioning), with dry-run support
failure_cases: health probe timeout or pod readiness failure triggers non-destructive rollback
coverage.failure_behavior: fail closed and execute non-destructive rollback on probe timeout

rollback.strategy: Non-destructive rollback preserving persistent volume claims and PostgreSQL statefulset

design_pack.security: Enforces non-root pod execution (runAsNonRoot: true), dropped Linux capabilities, Kubernetes Secrets for sensitive tokens, and tenant isolation via PostgreSQL RLS

contracts.db: PostgreSQL 16 with pgvector extension enabled and tenant RLS isolation
contracts.api: Core API exposes GET /api/v1/health returning 200 OK and Prometheus metrics at /api/v1/metrics
contracts.config: ConfigMap and Secret provide environment variables and database connection parameters

decisions: DEC-01: Decoupled AWS and GCP root Terraform modules into separate directory hierarchies for independent lifecycle management
DEC-02: Non-destructive rollback preserves stateful databases and volume claims, reverting only stateless deployment pods
DEC-03: Deployer CLI implemented as operator tooling under scripts/dev/plane_a_deployer.py adhering to tooling root conventions
learnings: Avoiding circular references between deployment execution summaries and step trail entries
Decoupled cloud provider Terraform structures prevent cloud vendor state leakage
non_goals: Replacing existing Plane B product deployers
Managing cloud vendor billing and IAM accounts outside defined terraform roles
Destructive tearing down of stateful databases during rollback
design_pack.ownership: Plane A platform operations team (owner: ops)
design_pack.data_model: PostgreSQL 16 relational tables with pgvector extension vector embeddings storage and MinIO object storage
guardrails: Fail-closed on missing credentials or invalid templates
No destructive destruction of production databases during rollback
invariants: INV-01: Persistent volume claims and HA database instances must retain data and survive workload rollback (reclaimPolicy: Retain)
INV-02: Pods run as non-root with dropped Linux capabilities and restricted privileges
INV-03: Cloud provisioning must support warm cluster deployments (<10m) and cold multi-cloud cluster rollouts (<25m)

tier_reasons: Plane A turnkey infrastructure provisioning and deployment automation
verification: End-to-end deployment test executing one_click_deploy.sh on test cluster and verifying healthy status endpoint.

NIT: Ensure `core/deploy_providers.py` edits are limited to infrastructure orchestration tooling rather than adding core platform runtime logic in Python (Language Rule).
MAJOR: AC-3 SLA of under 10 minutes for cloud VPC, managed EKS/GKE cluster, database provisioning, and platform deployment is architecturally unrealistic and will lead to deterministic deployment timeout failures.
Production Helm stack deploys single-instance PostgreSQL and MinIO subcharts without multi-AZ HA replication, failover strategy, or external secret management integration (Guardrail 2).
MINOR: `one_click_deploy.sh` lacks explicit dry-run (`terraform plan`) validation modes and target environment confirmation boundaries prior to resource provisioning (Guardrail 4).
BLOCKER: Rollback design specifies destructive `terraform destroy` / `helm uninstall` teardown without pre-destroy backup verifications or persistent volume retention policies, risking irrecoverable data loss (Guardrail 1).
SUMMARY: Design cannot be approved due to data loss risks during automated teardown and an unachievable provisioning SLA.
Primary risks include catastrophic storage destruction upon rollback and false-negative deployment failures from cloud infrastructure creation latency.
Architectural design for BI-PF-1555 meets all enterprise standards, security guardrails, and multi-cloud operational requirements.
Decoupled Terraform directory structures, non-destructive rollback mechanisms preserving stateful persistent volumes, and non-root security contexts ensure robust platform delivery.

NIT: Terraform variable declarations for database credentials lack input validation rules (e.g. minimum length or complexity constraints).
MAJOR: `scripts/dev/plane_a_deployer.py` health probe defaults to `http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/health` without setting up port-forwarding or resolving cloud load balancers, causing health checks to fail and trigger rollback on remote deployments.

Sensitive credentials (`change-in-production-vault`, static auth tokens) are hardcoded across Helm `values.yaml`, `secret.yaml`, and Terraform variable defaults without enforcing secret generation or external secret providers.
MINOR: Subprocess output handling in `plane_a_deployer.py` (`proc.stdout[-1000:]`) truncates CLI logs, which can obscure critical terraform and helm failure diagnostic details.
BLOCKER: `deploy/plane-a/terraform/aws/main.tf` creates `aws_eks_cluster` but omits `aws_eks_node_group` compute resources, causing all Helm stack pods on AWS to remain stuck in `Pending` state.

`deploy/plane-a/helm/product-forge/templates/configmap.yaml` hardcodes `POSTGRES_HOST` to the local StatefulSet service, leaving no configuration mechanism to connect `core-api` to the managed RDS/Cloud SQL databases provisioned by Terraform.
SUMMARY: Turnkey cloud deployment fails end-to-end on AWS/GCP due to missing EKS compute nodes, disconnected cloud database endpoints in Helm templates, and unrouted local health checks.
Add `aws_eks_node_group` to AWS Terraform, make Helm database endpoint configurable for managed DBs, and implement port-forwarding in the deployer script before approval.

MINOR: `scripts/dev/plane_a_deployer.py`: Truncating stdout logs to 5000 characters improves log visibility but can still drop critical error details during lengthy Terraform plan or Helm deployment failures.
BLOCKER: `deploy/plane-a/terraform/aws/main.tf`: `aws_iam_role.eks_node_role` lacks mandatory EKS worker node IAM policy attachments (`AmazonEKSWorkerNodePolicy`, `AmazonEKS_CNI_Policy`, `AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly`), causing node group creation or worker node joining to fail on AWS.
SUMMARY: The diff successfully addresses prior blockers by adding `aws_eks_node_group` to AWS Terraform and making `POSTGRES_HOST` configurable in the Helm chart.
Primary risk: Missing IAM policy attachments on the EKS node group role will prevent EKS nodes from bootstrapping successfully in AWS.
Verdict: PASS. The diff correctly resolves the prior blocker by attaching mandatory IAM node policies to the EKS worker role with explicit Terraform dependency ordering.
Residual risk: EKS node policy attachments use AWS managed broad policies; future hardening should evaluate fine-grained IAM scoping for production workloads.

NIT: `scripts/dev/deploy_plane_a.py` CLI wrapper relies on ambient environment Kubernetes context without offering an explicit `--kubeconfig` flag option.
MINOR: Default credential fields in `deploy/plane-a/helm/product-forge/values.yaml` should be validated as non-empty or supplied via ExternalSecrets to prevent insecure default deployments.
Multi-cloud Terraform definitions in `deploy/plane-a/terraform/` lack explicit state locking backend patterns, relying on outer wrapper execution to prevent state corruption.
SUMMARY: Provisioning architecture for Plane A platform deployment safely isolates stateful persistent volumes during rollback and complies with platform language rules.
Overall design meets all acceptance criteria with minimal risks; recommended minor hardening covers Helm default secrets and remote state lock definitions.
